newsitem.title: CHINA: China capital garbage dump triggers rare protest.
newsitem.headline: China capital garbage dump triggers rare protest.

text.p: Dozens of residents in a Beijing suburb on Wednesday staged a rare and daring protest against a nearby garbage dump they say is polluting their air and groundwater and making local people ill.
About 50 residents in Shangzhuang suburb in Beijing's northwestern Haidian district blocked the road to the garbage dump with cars and bicycles and unfurled banners demanding its closure.
"When the wind blows from the northwest it's really disgusting and makes us throw up," said one resident who gave his surname as Tao.
Protesters said they launched daily demonstrations six days ago after a petition they sent to local Haidian environmental authorities on June 2 demanding the dump's closure went unanswered.
"As people we have basic human rights," one man said. "I am outraged at this."
An official at the Beijing Environmental Protection Bureau said the authorities were now investigating the situation and would work out a solution within a few days.
"We have been to the site several times and had contact with the residents' representative," an official said by telephone. He declined to give further details.

Such public protests have been rare in China since the army crushed student-led protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square on June 3-4, 1989 with heavy loss of life. Demonstrations about the environment are virtually unheard of in China.
The demonstration comes at a time when Beijing is eager to present a facade of stability after the handover of the British colony of Hong Kong last Tuesday.
The 13.5-hectare (33-acre) dump was opened in March and had so far accumulated some 500,000 tonnes of trash that threatened to contaminate the local supply of drinking water, protesters said.
At least one resident, a pregnant woman, had been taken to hospital for nausea while many children and the elderly had fallen ill because of the smell, protesters said.
They accused the local government of lying to them about the site, telling residents a prison was being built there.
The dump came within 200 metres of the nearest residents in a district housing some 40,000-50,000 people, they said.

Police had threatened to break up the protest on Wednesday evening after hundreds of demonstrators over the last few days had forced several garbage trucks to turn back from the dump by lying across the road, they said.
"Unless they drive over us, we're not going anywhere," Tao said. "We might as well die early because we'll die later from this garbage."
